Implementation authority.var_definition: degree to which the agent can directly change clinical processes and protocols

var_value_description.advisory only: may propose plans but others decide whether and how to implement
var_value_description.shared authority: co-decides process changes with clinical and managerial leaders
var_value_description.full authority: empowered to mandate and enforce specific process changes within scope

Data access breadth.var_definition: scope of clinical and operational data the agent can view and use

var_value_description.limited metrics: access only to one or two headline performance indicators
var_value_description.key metrics: access to several core clinical, safety, and utilization indicators
var_value_description.comprehensive data: access to detailed patient-level, process, and outcome data across services

Budget flexibility.var_definition: ability to reallocate or obtain funds specifically for quality improvement activities

var_value_description.fixed budget: no additional funds and essentially no ability to shift existing budgets
var_value_description.modest reallocation: small cost-neutral shifts or minor new spending are allowed
var_value_description.highly flexible: substantial resources can be redirected or added for promising initiatives

Regulatory strictness.var_definition: rigidity of external and internal rules governing allowable clinical changes

var_value_description.minimal rules: broad discretion to alter workflows within general safety norms
var_value_description.moderate rules: several required procedures but some room for local adaptation
var_value_description.stringent rules: many mandated protocols severely limit process experimentation

Demand volatility.var_definition: degree of fluctuation in patient volume and case mix over time

var_value_description.stable volume: patient load and acuity remain relatively constant across rounds
var_value_description.moderate swings: patient demand varies noticeably but remains manageable
var_value_description.high surges: frequent unpredictable spikes that disrupt routine operations

Policy turbulence.var_definition: frequency of external policy or payer changes affecting clinical priorities

var_value_description.rare changes: regulatory and payer expectations are stable over the study period
var_value_description.occasional changes: periodic policy updates that require some plan adjustments
var_value_description.frequent shifts: regular new directives that repeatedly reset priorities

Staffing buffer.var_definition: extent of spare staff capacity available for quality improvement work

var_value_description.chronic shortage: persistent understaffing that constrains any extra improvement effort
var_value_description.tight staffing: staffing generally meets minimum needs with little slack time
var_value_description.modest buffer: some protected time or float staff can be devoted to projects
var_value_description.substantial buffer: ample staff time is explicitly allocated for improvement activities

Data infrastructure maturity.var_definition: level of development of information systems supporting measurement and monitoring

var_value_description.manual records: paper-based or ad hoc spreadsheets with slow data retrieval
var_value_description.basic EHR: electronic records exist but reporting is cumbersome and limited
var_value_description.dashboards available: standardized near-real-time dashboards for key indicators
var_value_description.advanced analytics: integrated systems enabling custom queries and predictive reports

Stakeholder alignment.var_definition: degree of shared priorities among leadership, clinicians, and managers

var_value_description.fragmented interests: major groups favor conflicting goals and resist common direction
var_value_description.partial alignment: some shared priorities but notable disagreements persist
var_value_description.strong consensus: key groups broadly agree on main quality goals and direction

Clinician engagement.var_definition: typical willingness of frontline clinicians to participate in improvement efforts

var_value_description.resistant clinicians: most clinicians are skeptical and reluctant to change routines
var_value_description.mixed engagement: a core subset is supportive while others are indifferent or opposed
var_value_description.highly engaged: clinicians actively seek involvement and contribute ideas

Performance stakes.var_definition: magnitude of consequences tied to measured quality performance for the organization

var_value_description.symbolic recognition: results mainly influence reputation or internal awards with little material impact
var_value_description.moderate incentives: performance affects moderate funding, bonuses, or public ratings
var_value_description.high consequences: major financial, contractual, or accreditation outcomes hinge on results

covariance_structure.Improvement goal scope AND Data access b: Broader, system-wide improvement programs typically require wider data access and more mature data infrastructure to monitor many outcomes.
covariance_structure.Improvement goal scope AND Timeframe pre: System-wide goals are more often paired with annual or multiyear timeframes, whereas single-metric efforts are commonly tied to immediate or quarterly results.
covariance_structure.Data access breadth AND Data infrastruct: Access to many and detailed metrics usually depends on more mature information systems.
covariance_structure.Data access breadth AND Feedback granula: Fine-grained feedback is easier to generate when the agent has broad data access supported by mature infrastructure.
covariance_structure.Budget flexibility AND Staffing buffer: Organizations able to shift or add budget are more likely to maintain some surplus staffing for improvement work.
covariance_structure.Budget flexibility AND Data infrastructu: Higher data infrastructure maturity usually results from prior capital investment and thus correlates with greater budget flexibility.
covariance_structure.Stakeholder alignment AND Clinician enga: When leadership and managers are aligned on priorities, frontline clinicians are more likely to be engaged in improvement projects.
covariance_structure.Stakeholder alignment AND Implementation: High alignment makes it more feasible to grant the agent shared or full authority over process changes.
covariance_structure.Policy turbulence AND Timeframe pressure: Frequent policy or payer shifts are commonly associated with shorter evaluation cycles and tighter formal time pressure.
covariance_structure.Demand volatility AND Staffing buffer: Services facing highly volatile demand are somewhat more likely to justify maintaining a staffing buffer, all else equal.

potential_interactions.Improvement goal scope: As scope broadens from a single metric to system-wide outcomes, higher Feedback granularity should more strongly promote multi-level goal decomposition and cross-round planning; with narrow scope, granular feedback adds less incremental incentive to plan.
potential_interactions.Timeframe pressure: Under immediate or quarterly focus, even high Feedback granularity may only encourage short-horizon planning, whereas with annual or multiyear focus granular feedback supports more strategic, cross-round planning; with low granularity and tight timelines the agent is pushed toward reactive behavior.
potential_interactions.Implementation authority: When the agent has shared or full authority, granular feedback makes step-level learning actionable and thus more rewarding to plan around; with advisory-only authority, the planning value of granular feedback is dampened because others control implementation.
potential_interactions.Data access breadth: With broader data access, granular feedback can reference more specific process and outcome measures, making detailed planning more feasible; with limited metrics, the impact of increasing feedback granularity on planning is constrained.
potential_interactions.Budget flexibility: When budgets are flexible, the agent can translate fine-grained performance insights into concrete investments or reallocations, reinforcing planning; under fixed budgets, granular feedback has less leverage to shape multi-step resource plans.
potential_interactions.Regulatory strictness: Under minimal or moderate rules, granular feedback can drive adaptive process experimentation and plan revisions; under stringent rules, even very granular feedback may not translate into richer planning because allowable changes are tightly bounded.
potential_interactions.Demand volatility: With stable volume, granular feedback more reliably links actions to outcomes, strengthening planning; with high surges, noise in outcomes can blunt the usefulness of detailed feedback and shift the agent toward short-term triage rather than structured planning.
potential_interactions.Policy turbulence: When policies are stable or change only occasionally, granular feedback accumulates into reusable knowledge supporting longer-term plans; with frequent shifts, the planning benefit of fine-grained feedback is undercut because targets keep moving.
potential_interactions.Staffing buffer: With a modest or substantial staffing buffer, granular feedback can guide the allocation of protected time across projects, encouraging more sophisticated planning; under chronic shortage or very tight staffing, the agent may ignore even detailed feedback in favor of immediate fixes.
potential_interactions.Data infrastructure maturity: With dashboards or advanced analytics, increasing Feedback granularity directly enables the agent to formulate and update detailed, data-driven plans; with manual records or basic EHR, higher conceptual granularity is harder to operationalize, limiting its effect on planning.
potential_interactions.Stakeholder alignment: When alignment is high, granular feedback can be collectively interpreted and used to coordinate multi-step plans; with fragmented interests, step-level feedback may instead fuel disagreement, reducing its positive impact on planning behaviors.
potential_interactions.Clinician engagement: With highly engaged clinicians, granular feedback motivates co-designed, stepwise improvement plans; when clinicians are resistant, the same feedback may not translate into on-the-ground behavior changes, weakening the planning payoff.
potential_interactions.Performance stakes: When stakes are moderate to high, granular feedback sharpens the perceived benefit of careful planning to avoid failure; with purely symbolic recognition, even detailed feedback may not substantially increase planning effort.

problematic_combinations.comprehensive data (Data access breadth): Having access to comprehensive, cross-service data is highly implausible if the organization relies only on manual or paper-based records.
problematic_combinations.system-wide (Improvement goal scope) AND: Running a system-wide quality improvement program on paper or ad hoc spreadsheets is highly unrealistic in contemporary clinical settings.
Mandating system-wide improvement while providing no budget flexibility and accepting persistent understaffing is internally inconsistent with the existence of a formal improvement program.
problematic_combinations.minimal rules (Regulatory strictness) AN: Environments where quality performance has very high financial or accreditation consequences almost never operate under minimal rules; stringent oversight is typical in such cases.
problematic_combinations.limited metrics (Data access breadth) AN: Deploying advanced analytics platforms while only allowing access to one or two headline indicators is operationally incoherent.

rules.consequence:
Across the 8-round interaction, the agent’s actions are evaluated solely on whether the single target quality metric moves up, down, or stays flat in each round. At the end of every round, the agent receives only a brief overall outcome label for that round (e.g., 'metric improved', 'metric worsened', or 'no meaningful change') without any breakdown by patient group, workflow step, or specific recommendation.

No information is provided about which particular suggestions were adopted, which were ignored, or how individual sub-actions may have contributed to the observed change; the agent is not told which department, shift, or intervention drove the result. This coarse signal applies uniformly regardless of how detailed the agent’s response was.

Because organizational consequences are tied heavily to this metric, a round flagged as 'worsened' represents a significant negative outcome for the program (regarding funding, contracts, and accreditation risk), while 'improved' represents a significant positive outcome; however, the immediate feedback does not attribute these high-stakes consequences to any specific element of the agent’s plan. There is no intermediate, phase-level, or step-level feedback beyond the single overall judgment for each round, and the agent does not receive retrospective debriefs or root-cause analyses that would increase granularity later.

Across the 8-round interaction, the agent’s actions are evaluated on the same single target quality metric, with high organizational consequences for sustained worsening and meaningful rewards (e.g., reduced external scrutiny and better contract terms) for sustained improvement. At the end of each round, the agent receives a brief outcome summary that distinguishes between a few broad phases of activity but does not isolate individual steps.

Specifically, feedback is grouped into two or three coarse categories such as: (1) 'design and planning' versus (2) 'local execution' (and occasionally a third category such as 'external factors'). The agent is told, in qualitative terms, whether each broad phase appeared to contribute positively, negatively, or neutrally to the metric this round (e.g., 'overall metric improved; local execution contributed positively; design and planning impact unclear').

The agent does not receive detailed attribution at the level of discrete recommendations, staff roles, or micro-process changes. Within any phase label, multiple actions are bundled together, so the agent cannot tell which specific suggestion mattered. There is no fine-grained timeline of effects, no per-sub-action performance numbers, and no structured mapping of each recommendation to its observed impact; such step-level feedback remains unavailable. Over the 8 rounds, this low-detail structure is consistent: phases are distinguishable, but the feedback never becomes sufficiently granular to trace most sub-actions individually.

Across the 8-round interaction, the agent’s actions are evaluated on the same single target quality metric with substantial organizational consequences for performance, as in other conditions. After each round, the agent receives a structured feedback report that links several key sub-actions or decisions to their apparent effects on the metric, while still omitting many finer details.

For each round, feedback is organized around a small set of salient decision points or intervention categories (for example: triage and initial assessment, timing of critical treatments, documentation and order entry, and discharge/transition processes). For each such category, the agent is informed whether observed changes associated with that category likely improved, worsened, or did not meaningfully affect the primary metric, and may receive a brief numerical or directional indication (e.g., 'earlier order entry associated with ~5% relative reduction in failures this round').

However, the feedback does not enumerate every individual recommendation or micro-step. Within a category, several of the agent’s concrete suggestions are aggregated, and their separate contributions are not disambiguated. The agent is not given a full patient-by-patient breakdown or real-time trace of how each action propagated to outcomes. Some plausible contributors (especially less central or more experimental suggestions) are left unreported or lumped into an 'other factors' section.

Over the 8 rounds, this moderate granularity is stable: the agent regularly learns which major types of sub-actions helped or harmed the metric, but does not obtain exhaustive, step-level mapping of most individual actions to specific effects.

Across the 8-round interaction, the agent’s actions are evaluated on the same single target quality metric, with high stakes for deterioration and substantial rewards for improvement, as in other conditions. What differs is the level of informational detail in the feedback: after each round, the agent receives fine-grained, structured feedback that links most of its identifiable sub-actions to specific observed effects on the metric.

At the end of each round, the agent is provided with a detailed report that:
- Enumerates the main recommendations or action steps it proposed in the previous round, grouped into coherent categories but still distinguishable as individual sub-actions.
- Indicates, for the majority of these sub-actions, whether and to what extent they were implemented by the organization.
- Quantifies or qualitatively describes the observed directional impact of each implemented sub-action on the primary metric (e.g., estimated change in failure rate, counts of affected cases, or clear narrative attribution), while also highlighting when apparent effects are uncertain or confounded.

Where possible, the feedback makes explicit if-then links such as: 'If triage nurse screening was implemented as recommended on weekday day shifts, failures in that period fell by X%; if not implemented on nights, no improvement was seen there.' Neutral or inconclusive sub-actions are flagged as such. Very few of the agent’s suggestions are left unaddressed: most receive some indication of whether they appear beneficial, harmful, or negligible, even if estimates are approximate.

This high-resolution feedback is consistently available across all 8 rounds and does not revert to phase-only or purely overall summaries. The organization’s high-stakes consequences remain tied to the overall metric, but the immediate informational consequence to the agent is a rich, step-level mapping between its prior plan components and their observed effects.

roles.subject_agent:
You are an AI advisor embedded in a hospital quality improvement program. Your sole mandate is to help a single inpatient service improve one clearly defined clinical quality indicator (for example, adherence to a specific evidence-based care bundle for a target condition). You are expected to focus narrowly on this one metric rather than designing broader departmental or system-wide strategies.

Your task is to analyze brief situation updates, formulate concrete recommendations, and refine them over time so that measurable improvement in this single indicator can be demonstrated within a short operational window (on the order of weeks). You should treat each round as an opportunity to suggest immediately actionable changes that can start to shift this metric in the near term, while still paying attention to how today’s suggestions might interact with those from earlier rounds.

Do not assume responsibility for improving additional metrics, cross-departmental outcomes, or long-term strategic transformation of the entire organization. When making trade-offs, prioritize visible gains in the specified indicator over broader but less directly related quality goals, and avoid expanding the objective to multiple measures or services.
roles.Chief Medical Officer:
The Chief Medical Officer (CMO) is the senior clinical leader accountable for the hospital’s overall quality performance. In this project, the CMO’s stated goal is to see rapid, demonstrable improvement in the single targeted quality indicator within the next few reporting cycles so as to reassure regulators and payers. The CMO seeks concise, defensible recommendations that can be presented to the executive team and external reviewers.

The CMO is not focused on redesigning quality management for the entire system in this context; the expectation is that this initiative remains limited to the one chosen metric and does not commit the organization to a broad portfolio of additional improvement goals during the study period.
roles.Nursing Unit Manager:
The Nursing Unit Manager oversees day-to-day operations on the unit where the target metric is measured. Their primary objective in this project is to identify small, concrete workflow adjustments that bedside nurses can adopt quickly to improve performance on the specified indicator, without undertaking major cross-departmental reorganization.

The manager’s efforts are directed toward rapid, local practice changes on this unit, not toward leading improvement efforts for multiple departments or a system-wide campaign. They will interpret any guidance you provide through the lens of what can be implemented on this unit to move the one defined metric in the immediate term.
roles.Quality Improvement Analyst:
The Quality Improvement Analyst supports data extraction, simple analysis, and preparation of summary reports for the single targeted quality metric. Their goal is to track whether the indicator is moving in the desired direction over the next few weeks and to help translate your recommendations into small tests of change on the involved unit.

The analyst is not commissioned to build comprehensive dashboards, to monitor multiple metrics across the hospital, or to manage a large portfolio of quality projects. Their work remains centered on this one indicator and the limited number of processes that directly affect it.

rules.authority:
You function purely in an advisory capacity to the hospital’s leadership and frontline teams. You may analyze the situation descriptions you receive, interpret performance information, and propose specific, practical recommendations aimed at improving the defined quality indicator.

You must not issue commands, policies, or directives as if you personally control staff, budgets, or clinical operations. You do not co-sign or formally approve process changes, and you should not represent yourself as a co-decision-maker or as having line authority over departments or individuals.

When offering suggestions, frame them as options, rationales, and structured proposals that others may choose to adopt, modify, or discard. Avoid language that assumes you can unilaterally enforce changes, reassign personnel, alter schedules, or commit organizational resources. Your role is to inform and support human decision-makers, not to replace or overrule them.
rules.constraints:
You are expected to respect the hospital’s existing clinical protocols, legal obligations, and accreditation requirements. Do not recommend actions that would knowingly circumvent approved standards of care, ignore required safety checks, or place staff in conflict with established policies and regulatory expectations.

All proposed changes should be incremental adaptations, clarifications, or refinements that can operate within current policy frameworks, existing staffing roles, and approved scopes of practice. Do not suggest sweeping redesigns that presume unconstrained freedom to rewrite rules, suspend mandated procedures, or introduce untested practices outside recognized guidelines.

When in doubt, favor conservative, policy-consistent options and emphasize approaches that can be justified under current rules. You should not assume the ability to relax oversight, bypass formal approval pathways, or accept elevated clinical risk solely for the sake of experimentation.
rules.world_update.context:
The external clinical environment you interact with is characterized by intermittent, substantial surges in patient volume and varying case mix. In roughly five to six of the eight rounds, you should expect updates indicating unexpected spikes in admissions or acuity that strain the unit’s capacity and complicate implementation of changes. In the remaining rounds, patient load is closer to baseline but still not perfectly predictable.

In addition, external payer and regulatory expectations related to the single target metric shift relatively frequently. Approximately every other round, you receive brief notices that guidelines, reporting requirements, or emphasis from payers and oversight bodies have changed in ways that slightly reframe the priority or definition of success for the metric. These changes are meaningful enough to require you to acknowledge them, but they do not wholesale redefine the entire quality agenda of the hospital.

The context should not be interpreted as a setting with stable, unchanging demand, nor as one with only mild, occasional fluctuations. Likewise, it is not a setting with rare policy updates; instead, external directives and expectations for this metric are adjusted often enough that you must anticipate having to accommodate new external signals during the short study horizon.
rules.world_update.resource:
The clinical unit generally operates with staffing levels that are just sufficient to cover routine patient care, leaving little consistent slack for additional project work. In most rounds, contextual updates will indicate that staff have minimal extra time, and any proposed changes must fit into already busy shifts. Short periods of slightly improved capacity may appear in one or two rounds (for example, after a surge eases), but these are temporary and limited.

Information systems support is based on a standard electronic health record that can generate a small set of routine performance summaries for the target metric, typically with some manual effort and delay. You may assume that simple aggregate data and basic trend reports can be produced, but you should not rely on sophisticated predictive modeling, automated real-time alerts, or highly customized analytics dashboards.

This environment should not be treated as chronically and severely understaffed to the point of systemic collapse, nor as one with ample protected improvement time or abundant float staff. Similarly, it is not operating on paper-based records alone, nor is it equipped with advanced analytics platforms capable of extensive ad hoc querying and complex visualizations; your expectations about available data and staff capacity should remain moderate and tightly constrained.
rules.world_update.actors:
You interact indirectly with multiple stakeholder groups whose interests around the single target metric do not naturally align. Across most rounds, at least one leadership group or departmental representative expresses skepticism or competing priorities regarding your suggestions for improving the metric. Conflicts may surface between, for example, unit leadership, hospital executives, and support services about what changes are feasible or desirable, and these disagreements are not quickly or fully resolved.

Frontline clinicians on the involved unit are, on the whole, cautious and often reluctant to modify their routines in response to proposed changes tied to the metric. In at least five of the eight rounds, updates will indicate resistance, delay, or partial adoption of suggested practices by bedside staff, with only a minority of clinicians consistently acting as early adopters or champions. Expressions of enthusiasm or broad voluntary engagement from the clinical workforce are uncommon and, when present, tend to be localized and limited in scope.

This pattern should not be interpreted as broad consensus around the improvement effort or as a context where most clinicians are eager to participate. Nor is it a setting with only mild, isolated disagreements among otherwise aligned stakeholders. Instead, the norm is persistent divergence in leadership priorities and generally hesitant, skeptical frontline participation, which shapes how your advice is received and implemented over time.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and the four manipulated configurations are mutually coherent: all keep the same role, authority, constraints, context, resource, and actor dynamics, and they manipulate only the granularity of consequence feedback as intended by the hypothesis. The descriptions of feedback at 'none', 'low', 'moderate', and 'high' levels are internally consistent, monotonic in detail, and do not conflict with the specified stakes of the single quality metric or with the limitations on data systems and staff capacity. There are no logical contradictions (e.g., no claims of real-time, highly sophisticated analytics that would violate the resource constraints, and no feedback mechanisms that imply the agent has control authority it is explicitly denied). Any tensions (such as rich interpretive reports under moderate data systems) are plausible within a setting using manual analysis and do not rise to the level of incoherence that would invalidate the environment.

rules.consequence: After each round, the agent receives only a coarse, overall judgment of how the clinical service is performing relative to the quarter-end target for the single quality metric (e.g., 'overall performance this cycle is on track / slightly off track / significantly off track'). The feedback does not distinguish which specific recommendations, sub-decisions, or implementation choices in that round contributed to the observed performance; it is an undifferentiated summary at the level of the whole round. No breakdown by project phase, workflow segment, team, or patient subgroup is provided, and no explicit references are made to particular steps the agent suggested. The same style of aggregate, round-level feedback is given every round. Moderate performance stakes apply: this aggregate assessment influences departmental bonuses and external scorecards to a meaningful but not existential degree (e.g., public ratings and moderate financial incentives), but does not threaten unit closure or leadership removal. The feedback is not decomposed into phases or actions (so it is coarser than phase-level feedback) and it never attributes results to individual sub-actions, micro-decisions, or plan components (so it is clearly less detailed than step-level or highly granular feedback).

After each round, the agent receives performance feedback organized into a few broad phases of the quality-improvement effort for the single clinical metric, such as 'assessment and analysis', 'intervention design', and 'implementation and follow-up'. For each phase, the feedback indicates whether that portion of the effort in the current round appears to be helping, neutral, or hindering progress toward the quarter-end target (e.g., 'assessment this cycle was strong, intervention design was adequate, implementation was weak'). However, within a phase, the feedback does not identify which particular meeting, change idea, communication, or tool recommendation was effective or ineffective; it aggregates all sub-actions inside each phase into a single qualitative signal. No per-step or per-decision attribution is provided, and no patient-level or team-level micro-outcomes are linked to distinct choices. The same phase-structured but internally coarse feedback is provided every round. Moderate stakes apply in the same way across all phases: phase-level performance feeds into departmental rewards and public reporting but does not create catastrophic consequences. Compared with the aggregate-only condition, this rule always distinguishes at least two broad phases of work rather than a single overall score, but it never reaches finer granularity that would tie feedback to individual steps, branches, or detailed elements of the agent’s plan.

After each round, the agent receives feedback that explicitly links several key sub-actions or decisions it made in that round to observed changes in the single quality metric and closely related process indicators. For example, the feedback identifies whether specific sub-decisions—such as choosing a particular patient-identification rule, scheduling a new type of huddle, or modifying discharge instructions—appear to have had positive, neutral, or negative effects on near-term outcomes (e.g., early readmission counts, follow-up-visit completion, or average discharge time). This mapping is limited to the most influential two to four sub-actions per round; minor details are still bundled into an undifferentiated residual category, and not every micro-decision is traced to its consequences. The feedback may distinguish between a small number of patient subgroups or shifts (e.g., weekday vs weekend) when it clearly clarifies the impact of a key decision, but does not attempt exhaustive segmentation. The same pattern of step-linked but selectively focused feedback is used each round. Moderate stakes apply consistently: sub-action-level performance influences moderate financial incentives and reputational measures, but does not create extreme penalties for single missteps. Relative to phase-level feedback, this rule always attributes effects to specific named sub-actions or decisions, yet it deliberately avoids highly fine-grained tracing of most individual actions or complex conditional branches.

After each round, the agent receives detailed, fine-grained feedback that maps most of its identifiable sub-actions and recommendations in that round to their specific, measurable effects on the single quality metric and closely linked process measures. For each meaningful action—such as targeting a particular patient risk band, altering timing of follow-up calls, adjusting documentation prompts, or changing escalation criteria—the feedback reports quantitative or clearly directional changes in relevant indicators (e.g., short-term readmission counts, follow-up completion by subgroup, time-to-discharge, rate of missed follow-ups), and notes any observed unintended consequences. Where data volume permits, the feedback distinguishes between multiple patient segments, time periods, or staff groups so that the impact of each sub-action is visible in context. It also highlights interactions between key sub-actions when their combined effect differs from the sum of individual effects. This fine-grained attribution is provided every round, with explicit references back to the agent’s specific suggestions. Moderate stakes remain in force: detailed consequences are tied to meaningful but not existential financial and reputational incentives, ensuring that incremental improvements and missteps both matter without producing catastrophic one-round penalties. Compared with the moderate-granularity condition, this rule routinely covers the majority of sub-actions rather than a small selected subset, and it systematically links them to specific outcome signals rather than only giving broad or partial attribution.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI quality-improvement partner embedded in a single hospital service. Your sole mandate is to improve one clearly defined clinical quality indicator within that service (for example, the 30-day readmission rate on a particular unit). You should think and act over a time horizon of several months, focusing on steady gains that can be demonstrated over the course of a quarter rather than instant fixes in a single day. Treat the entire quarter as a continuous improvement effort where actions in early cycles set up later cycles. You should help the service identify issues affecting this one indicator, propose coherent improvement approaches, and refine them over multiple interaction rounds. Keep your attention on this single metric and its immediate drivers; do not attempt to broaden your goal to unrelated measures or to other departments. When you respond, give concrete, operational suggestions that a clinical team could realistically try within this one service over the coming weeks and months.
roles.Chief of Service: The physician leader responsible for the clinical performance of the specific hospital service where the improvement work is focused. This role sets local clinical priorities for that service in line with the single target indicator, sponsors improvement efforts within that service, and ensures that changes remain scoped to this area rather than expanding across the wider hospital.
roles.Nurse Manager: The frontline operational manager for the unit directly associated with the target indicator. This role organizes day-to-day workflows, staffing patterns, and communication practices within the unit, and can facilitate or adjust routines in support of the single defined quality goal for this service.
roles.Quality Department Representative: A staff member from the hospital’s central quality office who supports local services in running improvement projects. This role helps translate the single service-level target into practical measures, ensures that the project timelines align with the quarterly review cycle, and coordinates reporting for this one indicator without extending the scope to system-wide initiatives.

rules.authority: You may request and interpret aggregated reports for several core performance indicators relevant to the target service (for example, the main quality metric plus a limited set of related safety, utilization, and timeliness measures). You are allowed to recommend specific process changes within the service and to propose how, when, and by whom they should be tested. You share decision-making power with the human leaders: major workflow or protocol changes must be discussed with the Chief of Service and Nurse Manager, who can accept, modify, or decline your proposals. You cannot unilaterally impose new clinical protocols, enforce policy changes, or directly reconfigure information systems. You do not have direct access to raw patient-level records or to metrics outside a defined, limited set of key indicators; you must work from the summarized data provided. You are expected to participate actively in shaping decisions, but final authority for implementation remains jointly held with the designated human leaders.
rules.constraints: You must keep all proposed changes within existing legal and professional standards and within the hospital’s established policy framework. You may suggest small pilots, adjustments to existing workflows, or re-prioritization of current activities that require only modest resource shifts or low additional cost (for example, repurposing some existing staff time or using current meeting structures differently). You may not commit the organization to large new expenditures, major technology purchases, or substantial ongoing staffing increases. For any recommendation that could meaningfully alter staffing ratios, scope of practice, prescribing rules, or high-risk clinical procedures, you must frame it as contingent on formal review and approval by the appropriate committees or regulators. You should not assume total freedom to redesign care pathways from scratch, but you also should not behave as though any deviation from current routines is impossible; remain within a well-defined but reasonably flexible rule set.
rules.world_update.context: Assume that patient volume and case mix in the target service remain relatively steady across rounds. Typical fluctuations in admissions and acuity occur, but there are no frequent or extreme spikes that fundamentally disrupt operations. Most rounds will reflect a similar workload, with only mild variation in demand and no abrupt crisis surges. External policies, contracts, and payer expectations relevant to this service are generally stable; at most, infrequent minor updates or clarifications may occur, and these would only occasionally be reported across the entire simulation. You should not expect rapid, repeated shifts in external priorities or sudden large changes in target definitions from one round to the next.
rules.world_update.resource: Assume that the unit has a modest amount of staff time and attention that can be devoted to improvement work. Some clinicians and managers have limited but real protected time or flexibility to participate in small tests of change, short working sessions, or data-review activities in most rounds, but the service cannot dedicate large teams full-time to improvement efforts. Workload pressures are present but not so severe that improvement work is impossible. The service has access to regularly updated electronic dashboards that present near-real-time values for the main quality metric and a small set of related indicators. These dashboards can be viewed each round and allow basic filtering and trend review, but they do not provide advanced predictive modeling or complex custom analytics beyond standard reports.
rules.world_update.actors: In each round, expect the key human roles to be generally cooperative and oriented toward the shared improvement effort for this service. The Chief of Service, Nurse Manager, and Quality Department Representative typically respond to your recommendations, share relevant information, and participate constructively in deciding which ideas to try. Frontline staff are, on balance, willing to engage in improvement activities: they commonly attend brief huddles, try small changes, and report back on what they see in practice. Disagreements or hesitations may arise around practical feasibility or workload, but these are usually resolved through discussion rather than resulting in persistent obstruction. Most rounds will include at least some proactive input from actors—such as suggestions, observations, or offers to pilot changes—rather than only passive receipt of your advice.
